questions.q: How does Spring Security apply its protections to web requests?
o: A chain of servlet filters that runs before the controller
Rewriting the bytecode of controllers
Editing the database schema at startup
Asking for a password on every single call
questions.w: `DelegatingFilterProxy` hands each request to the `SecurityFilterChain`. Filters handle authentication, CSRF, headers and authorization.

questions.q: Which interface turns a username into a user with a password hash and authorities?
o: `UserDetailsService`
`PasswordEncoder`
`AuthenticationEntryPoint`
`SecurityContextHolder`
questions.w: `PasswordEncoder` (use `BCryptPasswordEncoder` or `DelegatingPasswordEncoder`) verifies the supplied password against the stored hash.

questions.q: Where does Spring Security store the current authenticated user for a request?
o: In the `SecurityContext`, via `SecurityContextHolder`
In a static field that is declared in the controller class
In the database only, and it is read again for every call
In the URL of the request, as a query parameter
questions.w: By default it is held in a thread-local, and for sessions it is saved in the HTTP session between requests.

questions.q: A stateless REST API uses bearer tokens. What should you do with CSRF protection?
o: Usually disable it, as there is no cookie session to forge
Keep it on and send the CSRF token inside a cookie
Replace it with a much longer password for each user
Switch on HTTP Basic authentication in its place
questions.w: CSRF exploits browsers sending cookies automatically. With the token in an `Authorization` header it does not apply. Keep CSRF for cookie sessions.

o: It checks authorization before the method runs, via a proxy
It logs the current user in as an administrator
It creates a new ADMIN role in the database at startup
It encrypts the value that the method returns
questions.w: Enable with `@EnableMethodSecurity`. Like other proxy features it is bypassed by self-invocation.

questions.q: How does a Spring Boot resource server validate a JWT bearer token?
o: It verifies the signature with the issuer's keys and checks `exp`, `iss` and `aud`
It sends the user's password to the issuer for each request
It trusts any token as long as the length looks right
It stores every token in a database before it accepts it
questions.w: Configure `spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri` and the keys are discovered from the JWKS endpoint.

questions.q: Which is the correct handling of a user who is logged in but calls an endpoint they have no right to?
o: Return `403 Forbidden`
Return `401 Unauthorized`
Always return `404 Not Found`
Log the user out
questions.w: `401` means unauthenticated. `403` means authenticated but not permitted. Sometimes `404` is used deliberately to hide existence.

questions.q: Why shouldn't you store passwords with a plain SHA-256 hash?
o: It is fast, so attackers can test billions of guesses a second
SHA-256 is far too slow to be used at login time
The SHA-256 output is too long to be stored in a column
Spring Security cannot use SHA-256 for any purpose
questions.w: Slow adaptive hashes make brute force expensive. `DelegatingPasswordEncoder` also lets you upgrade algorithms over time.
